title: The Frankfurt School
keyWorks: T. Adorno and M. Horkheimer, Dialectic of Enlightenment (1947)
E. Fromm, The Art of Loving (1956)
E. Fromm, To Have or to Be? (1976)
summary: The Frankfurt School was a circle of philosophers and sociologists who, from the 1920s on, worked around the Institute for Social Research in Frankfurt. They combined philosophy, sociology and psychoanalysis to understand how the structure of society shapes a person’s inner life. Erich Fromm, Theodor Adorno, Max Horkheimer and Herbert Marcuse asked, in different ways but with equal persistence: why, in a society of abundance, do people so often feel unfree and unhappy?
onEmotions: For the Frankfurt School, feelings are not only a private matter: they reflect the society we live in. Fromm spoke of “social character” — the typical traits a society cultivates in people so that they fit into it well. Adorno and Marcuse showed how the culture of entertainment and consumption shapes our desires and even our idea of freedom. From this follows an important and often relieving thought: your anxiety, fatigue or emptiness is not necessarily just your personal failure. To understand the social causes of a feeling is to stop blaming yourself for it and to hear in it the voice of a living person.

anxiety.text: In 1941 Erich Fromm asked: why does freedom frighten us so? If an unstable world makes you anxious, you are living inside that question. In Escape from Freedom he showed that modern people, released from old ties — estate, community, tradition — gained “freedom from.” But with it came loneliness and insecurity: now everything depends on you, and there seems to be nothing to lean on. Fromm described how people try to escape this anxiety — by submitting to authority or dissolving into the crowd (“automaton conformity”). In To Have or to Be? he added: if a person defines themselves by what they have — money, status, relationships — they will inevitably be anxious, since all of it can be lost. Fromm saw the way out not in new armor but in “freedom to”: in living engagement, love, creativity. Your anxiety is not a defect; in part, it is the price of freedom.
anxiety.practice: As Fromm advised in The Art of Loving, sit comfortably, close your eyes and for a minute simply follow your breathing without trying to change it. When the worry “what might I lose” comes up, silently label it “having” and return to the breath.

quote.text: If I am what I have and if what I have is lost, who then am I?
quote.author: Erich Fromm

fear.text: “The fully enlightened earth radiates disaster triumphant” — so begins Dialectic of Enlightenment, written by two refugees from Nazism. There is no shame in being afraid today: fear is one of the most ancient human experiences. Its authors, Adorno and Horkheimer, start from the idea that reason and science sought from the very beginning to free people from fear of nature. But their conclusion is unsettling: a society built on control over nature and people gives rise to new fears — of an impersonal system, of turning out to be “superfluous.” Fromm, in Escape from Freedom, said that many people fear freedom itself and are ready to give it up for a sense of security. Then your fear is not just an inner problem: it often responds to the real fragility of life in the modern world. Acknowledging this means you can stop thinking of yourself as “too sensitive” and see that many people fear the same thing.
fear.practice: Ask someone close — a friend, a colleague: “Does this scare you too?” The Frankfurt thinkers taught us to hear a shared fear inside a private one, and another person’s “yes” often makes it lighter.

sadness.text: “The need to lend a voice to suffering is a condition of all truth,” Adorno wrote. Your sadness may be not a glitch in your mood but just such a voice: an honest response to what is happening. In One-Dimensional Man (1964), Herbert Marcuse described the “happy consciousness” — an attitude in which consumer society invites us to be content and not ask unnecessary questions. In such a world, sadness is easily mistaken for a malfunction to be fixed as quickly as possible. Marcuse, on the contrary, valued “the power of negative thinking” — the ability to see that reality could be different and better. If so, your sadness may be a form of clarity: you are noticing what not everyone wants to notice. It doesn’t need to be urgently replaced with positivity — it can be given a voice.
sadness.practice: Write, without softening it: “I am sad because…” — and leave the sentence without a consoling conclusion. Adorno distrusted hasty reconciliation.

quote.text: The need to lend a voice to suffering is a condition of all truth.
quote.author: Theodor Adorno

grief.text: Fromm loved a distinction he put in the title of a book: to have or to be. When you lose someone, that distinction suddenly stops being theory. Grief keeps no correct timeline. In the “having” mode we treat people and things as possessions; in the “being” mode, as a living relationship in which we ourselves take part. For Fromm, what has been lost is not something you “had” but something you lived by — which is why the pain is so great. But everything lived in the mode of being — love, attention, shared moments — has become part of who you are and cannot simply be taken away. In Eros and Civilization, Marcuse wrote of memory as a force that preserves the experience of happiness once lived. To remember is not to be stuck; it is a way of going on loving.
grief.practice: Today, do one small thing the way the one you lost used to do it: brew the tea, hum the tune, walk the familiar route. In the mode of being, memory lives not in keeping but in doing.

loneliness.text: In The Art of Loving (1956) Fromm recalls Adam and Eve: having eaten from the tree of knowledge, they see themselves as separate for the first time — and are ashamed. That, for Fromm, is where loneliness grows from: awareness of separateness is the deepest source of anxiety, and the wish to overcome it the deepest need. If you feel lonely now, you are touching the oldest human question. He described false ways of escaping loneliness: dissolving into a group, living “like everyone else,” filling time with consumption. Such conformity gives a sense of belonging, but not real closeness. The true answer, for Fromm, is love as an active relationship in which two people unite while remaining themselves. And one more relieving thought from the school: loneliness is largely produced by a society in which relationships increasingly become exchanges. Your feeling is not a verdict on you but a longing for living connection.
loneliness.practice: Call or message one person and ask not “how are you?” but about something you are genuinely curious about in their life. For Fromm, closeness begins with living interest.

anger.text: Marcuse called it the “Great Refusal” — the capacity to say “no” to whatever makes life poorer. Your anger may carry such a “no,” and sometimes there is truth in it. In The Anatomy of Human Destructiveness (1973), Erich Fromm distinguished two kinds of aggression. “Benign,” defensive aggression serves life: it arises when your boundaries, dignity or freedom are threatened. “Malignant” aggression is destructive; it grows out of powerlessness and alienation. In this light, your anger may be a signal: something is constraining you or others, and you feel it. What matters is not to suppress it or turn it against yourself, but to understand what exactly it is protecting — and to find a form for that which harms neither you nor anyone else.
anger.practice: On an in-breath clench your fists as hard as you can, and release them on the out-breath — three times. Fromm told apart anger that defends life from anger that destroys: let your body voice the first before you speak.

shame.text: Picture a shop window where people are on display instead of goods, each with a price tag. Fromm thought market society quietly puts us in such a window. If you feel ashamed now, it’s worth asking whose hand wrote the tag. Fromm described the “marketing orientation” — a type of character cultivated by a society in which everything is for sale. A person begins to perceive themselves as a commodity: what matters is not who they are but how well they “sell” — how attractive, successful, in demand they are. Hence a distinctly modern shame: as if you were not “competitive” enough as a person. In Minima Moralia (1951), Adorno showed how the pressure of society penetrates the most private corners of life. So part of your shame may not be personal guilt but a consequence of yardsticks imposed on everyone. You can ask yourself: on whose scale am I grading myself right now?
shame.practice: Read Adorno’s line from Minima Moralia slowly aloud: “The splinter in your eye is the best magnifying glass.” Consider what your shame, like that splinter, lets you see in the yardsticks around you.

guilt.text: “Wrong life cannot be lived rightly,” Adorno wrote in Minima Moralia, and this harsh sentence is unexpectedly consoling. Guilt can be justified, and it can be out of all proportion. In Man for Himself (1947), Erich Fromm distinguished two kinds of conscience. The “authoritarian conscience” is the internalized voice of an external authority — parents, bosses, society; it makes us feel guilty for disobedience. The “humanistic conscience” is our own voice, calling us to our own growth and to fullness of life. Hence Adorno’s thought: in an unjustly ordered world there is no flawless life. So part of your guilt is not a personal failure but a consequence of the fact that flawlessness is unattainable in principle. This doesn’t cancel responsibility for specific actions, but it lets you tell it apart from endless self-accusation.
guilt.practice: Say your guilty sentence aloud, then repeat it in the voice of the person you first heard it from. Fromm would ask: is this your humanistic conscience speaking, or the authoritarian one?

quote.text: Wrong life cannot be lived rightly.
quote.author: Theodor Adorno

envy.text: Marcuse proposed a simple and awkward test: which of my desires are really mine, and which were sold to me? Envy, in a world where other people’s success is always on display, is a good occasion to run it. In One-Dimensional Man, Marcuse distinguished “true” from “false” needs. False needs are those imposed from outside and sustained by advertising and consumer culture: wanting what others have, looking and living the same way. Fromm spoke of the “having” mode, in which a person’s worth is measured by what they possess, and comparison becomes endless. This means envy is often fed not by your real desires but by a system that constantly shows you what you don’t have. This doesn’t make you a petty person. But you can ask: do I really want this — or was I taught to want it?
envy.practice: Imagine you have the thing you envy, but no one will ever know. Do you still want it? This is how Marcuse separated true needs from false ones.

emptiness.text: You can dutifully do what’s required and buy what you’re supposed to — and never once feel yourself the living source of your own actions. Fromm called this alienation: a person becomes not the author of their life but a performer of roles written by others. Hence an emptiness that new things don’t fill — and it doesn’t mean something is wrong with you. Marcuse showed that a society of abundance can satisfy many needs and still leave people unfree. Against this Fromm set the “productive orientation” — a life in which you yourself create, love, think. In other words, emptiness is not the absence of you but a sign that the living part of you wants more than consumption.
emptiness.practice: Make one small thing with your hands from start to finish — brew tea properly, sew on a button, water a plant. Fromm called this productive activity: you are its source.

confusion.text: “The whole life of the individual is nothing but the process of giving birth to himself,” Fromm wrote in The Sane Society. Confusion, when ready-made answers are growing scarce, may be part of that birth rather than a breakdown. Fromm saw this as the flip side of freedom. When external authorities and traditions stop telling people how to live, they gain room to move — and at the same time lose their footing. In Escape from Freedom Fromm showed how tempting it is at such moments to grab hold of someone who will tell you what to think, or simply do “what everyone does.” But he believed another path was possible — “freedom to”: a gradual, independent discovery of what you value. And birth is never clear from the first step. Then confusion is not a failure but a place where this slow process can begin.
confusion.practice: Walk for five minutes with no route and no headphones, like Benjamin’s flâneur, and let the question “what matters to me now?” walk beside you without demanding an answer.

fatigue.text: “I have no hobby,” Adorno declared defiantly in his essay “Free Time”: he refused to let even rest become one more occupation. If you are burned out, it is often not a personal weakness but the predictable result of a way of life. In Eros and Civilization (1955), Herbert Marcuse introduced the concept of the “performance principle”: in modern society a person’s worth is measured by their efficiency. He also spoke of “surplus repression” — restrictions not needed for survival that serve to maintain a particular order of work and consumption. In the same essay Adorno observed that even rest is often organized as a continuation of work: it has to be “spent productively.” If so, your burnout says not that you aren’t trying hard enough but that the demands exceed human measure. Rest is not a reward for merit; it is your right.
fatigue.practice: For five minutes, switch off everything that buzzes and glows, and sit without “spending the time productively.” Adorno, who had no hobby, would approve of such idleness.

boredom.text: “As soon as the film begins, it is quite clear how it will end,” Adorno and Horkheimer observed. Boredom can be agonizing even amid plenty of entertainment — and perhaps precisely because of that predictability. Their concept of the “culture industry” explains why: entertainment is produced as a standardized commodity, and leisure comes to resemble work — just as monotonous and predictable. In his essay “Free Time,” Adorno linked boredom to unfreedom: when a person can’t truly dispose of themselves, their free time doesn’t become free. Marcuse described “one-dimensionality” — a life in which everything is offered in advance and there is no room for anything else. In this light, boredom is not your inability to enjoy yourself but, perhaps, a reaction to a world that is too uniform. A desire for something real, something not bought, may live in it.
boredom.practice: Do one thing today that has neither use nor audience: build a little house of matches, sing, fold a paper boat. Marcuse saw a piece of freedom in such play.

joy.text: Fromm wrote in To Have or to Be? that joy is what we experience in the process of growing nearer to the goal of becoming ourselves. Your joy can be trusted. Fromm distinguished it from pleasure. Pleasure, or thrill, in the having mode passes quickly and demands ever new stimuli — purchases, entertainment, impressions. Joy, for Fromm, accompanies living, productive activity: when you create, love, understand, take part. It is not a flash followed by a slump but more like a steady glow, a companion of being. Marcuse, for his part, insisted that the pursuit of happiness is a legitimate human demand, not a whim. So your joy doesn’t need to be justified or “earned”: it tells you that right now you are truly alive and engaged.
joy.practice: Tell someone about your joy — not to boast but to share it. Fromm believed that in the mode of being, joy doesn’t shrink from this but grows.

love.text: Fromm opens The Art of Loving (1956) with a question: why do we spend years learning music or medicine, yet assume we already know how to love? For him love is not a pleasant feeling we happen to “fall into.” It is an art and an active power; it requires discipline, concentration, patience. He named its four foundations: care, responsibility, respect and knowledge of the other. Respect is the ability to see a person as they are and to want them to grow in their own way, not in the way that suits you. Fromm distinguished immature love, built on need, from mature love, in which two people unite while preserving themselves. Your tenderness is not weakness but the beginning of this art.
love.practice: Spend five minutes today with someone you love in full concentration — no phone, no side tasks. Fromm considered concentration the first exercise in the art of loving.

quote.text: Immature love says: “I love you because I need you.” Mature love says: “I need you because I love you.”
quote.author: Erich Fromm

gratitude.text: Fromm would probably have seen in gratitude the other side of what he called “the highest expression of potency” — giving. He didn’t write about it separately, but the warmth you feel would have made sense to him. In The Art of Loving he observed that for the marketing character, giving means being deprived, so such a person gives only in exchange. For the “productive” character, however, giving is the highest expression of one’s own strength and vitality: in giving, a person experiences their own fullness. Gratitude is the mirror side of such giving: you receive something not as a transaction but as a sign of a living relationship. In a society where so much has been turned into calculation, the ability to give thanks without keeping score is a small expression of the mode of “being.” It connects you with others not through debt but through generosity.
gratitude.practice: Today, thank one person for something specific and unobvious — not for a favor but for who they are. With no calculation of return.

hope.text: A crouching tiger that doesn’t pace about but will leap when the moment comes — this is how Fromm pictured hope. If hope is hard to hold on to right now, this image may help. In The Revolution of Hope (1968), Erich Fromm described it with subtlety. Hope is not passive waiting for someone to do everything for us, nor a frantic forcing of events that have not yet ripened. Hope, for Fromm, is an inner readiness for what is not yet born. Marcuse, closing his most critical book, One-Dimensional Man, nevertheless left room for hope by quoting Walter Benjamin. This means hope doesn’t require certainty of a good outcome: it is a way of staying alive and open, even when the future is unclear.
hope.practice: Read aloud the line from Benjamin with which Marcuse ended One-Dimensional Man: “It is only for the sake of those without hope that hope is given to us.” Stay for a minute with whatever it stirs in you.

quote.text: Only for the sake of those without hope is hope given to us.
quote.author: Walter Benjamin
quote.source: essay “Goethe’s Elective Affinities”; Herbert Marcuse ends One-Dimensional Man (1964) with this line

nostalgia.text: Marcuse saw memory as a subversive force: whoever remembers happiness once lived knows that life can be better than it is now — so he wrote in Eros and Civilization. The warm, wistful longing for the past that you feel is entirely natural. In other words, nostalgia is not merely a retreat backward but a secret knowledge of what fullness can be. But in the spirit of Adorno and Horkheimer’s analysis of the “culture industry,” one can add a caution: the entertainment industry knows how to sell the past as a commodity — packaged, edited, painless. So it helps to distinguish your own memories from ready-made images of “the good old days.” Your nostalgia can hint at what you are missing now — and that is a valuable hint.
nostalgia.practice: Hold an object from that time — a photo, a book, a cup — for a minute. Ask: is this my own memory, or a ready-made image of “the good old days”?

craving.text: Marcuse coined a heavy term for this — “repressive desublimation” — but its meaning is simple: the system readily offers quick pleasures that relieve tension for a minute and leave the real need hungry. A sharp “I want it right now” can be almost unbearable, and there is nothing shameful in it. Adorno and Horkheimer wrote that consumer culture constantly promises satisfaction and constantly postpones it. Then a craving is not only your weakness: a real need often speaks through it, one that has been handed a substitute. A craving is like a wave: it rises, peaks and subsides. While it passes, you can ask yourself what this need is really asking for.
craving.practice: While the wave of craving rises, put a hand on your belly and breathe slowly, counting out-breaths to ten. On each out-breath silently ask, “What am I really missing?” — without demanding an answer.

addiction.text: “The deepest need of man is the need to overcome his separateness,” Fromm wrote in The Art of Loving (1956). When life has long revolved around one thing, it is exhausting — and it is not a moral failure. Among the ways people try to do this, he named “orgiastic states,” including alcohol and drugs, and stressed that these are understandable attempts, but afterward a person feels even more separate, and the circle closes. In The Sane Society (1955), Fromm added that much suffering is a response to a society in which it is hard to be alive and connected to others. If so, addiction is a distorted search for connection, not a flaw of character. And so the way out, for Fromm, lies not in self-punishment but in a gradual return to living relationships.
addiction.practice: Tell one person with whom you feel less separate how you really are. A mutual-help group, where others know this circle from the inside, can also be such a listener.

hangover.text: Fromm would probably call the morning after a return of separateness: yesterday’s merging has come apart, leaving anxiety, shame, fragments of last night. You are not alone in this. In The Art of Loving he described how states of intoxication briefly give a sense of union and freedom, after which the opposite arrives — a sharp feeling of separateness, which is experienced as shame and anxiety. In Eros and Civilization (1955), Marcuse spoke of the “performance principle”: society expects us to be composed and efficient again by morning. Hence a double weight — you feel bad, and you’re not allowed to feel bad. If we follow Marcuse, your “moral hangover” is partly fear of being judged by that principle. Today you can simply allow yourself to be a person who feels bad, without demanding an immediate account from yourself.
hangover.practice: Drink a glass of water slowly, noticing each sip — let the morning begin not with a report to the “performance principle” but with care for your body. The question “what happened last night” can wait an hour.

euphoria.text: “Beauty is nothing but the promise of happiness”: Adorno loved these words of Stendhal and kept returning to them. A sudden high, when everything seems possible, is a vivid experience, and there’s no need to be ashamed of it. In Eros and Civilization, Marcuse wrote that in moments of joy, in art and imagination, a person glimpses a different, freer life — one that everyday existence usually pushes aside. In this light, euphoria may be not an illusion but a brief flash of knowledge: yes, life can feel like this. The Frankfurt thinkers also soberly noted that society knows how to sell such flashes as commodities. So it is worth distinguishing where the high came from. But the image of what is possible that it showed you can be carefully kept.
euphoria.practice: Close your eyes and imagine what an ordinary Tuesday would look like with a little of this “promise of happiness” in it. One detail — then open your eyes.

crash.text: “Amusement under late capitalism is the prolongation of work,” Adorno and Horkheimer observed drily: it exists to restore your strength for the next working day. If a drop has come after a celebration, a success or a vivid evening, it is not your fault. The celebration is built into the schedule in advance, and a return to the usual rhythm inevitably follows. So the comedown is not only chemistry or character but also a collision with the sharp contrast between a moment of freedom and an everyday life where there is little freedom. Understanding this means seeing that you are longing not for the high itself but for a life with more aliveness in it. That longing is not weakness but a sign that you need this aliveness.
crash.practice: Put on one song from that evening and listen to it all the way through, doing nothing else. Let the living part of the high look into an ordinary day too.

panic.text: Marcuse would probably put it like this: society trains us to treat the body as an instrument that must work without fail. And then your heart pounds, your breathing falters, it feels as if something irreparable is about to happen — this is genuinely frightening. The Frankfurt thinkers didn’t write about panic, but their view of the body helps here. When the body suddenly slips out of control, it is especially frightening — after all, we were taught that control is the norm. This means instead of only fighting your body, you can for a minute take its side, as you would the side of a living creature that is scared. A wave like this usually rises, peaks, and within a few minutes begins to subside.
panic.practice: Take your body’s side: put both feet on the floor, feel the support, and make each out-breath longer than the in-breath — slowly, several times, as if cooling hot tea. You are not repairing an instrument; you are calming something alive.

dread.text: In The Jargon of Authenticity (1964), Adorno mocked philosophers who spoke of death solemnly, as if the fear of it were the central truth about the human being. If you are hit by the question “what’s the point of it all?” and a sense of the abyss, it is an honest experience — but there is no need to heroize it. Adorno thought this lofty acceptance of finitude too easily turns into resignation to the way the world is arranged. In Eros and Civilization, Marcuse wrote that finitude is inevitable, but culture should not turn death into an ideal. Fromm contrasted “necrophilia” — an attraction to everything dead and mechanical — with “biophilia,” the love of what is alive. In other words, dread before the abyss is not a verdict but one side of a deep attachment to life. The Frankfurt thinkers looked for the answer to “what for?” in what is alive: in people, in work, in love.
dread.practice: Look out the window or step outside for a minute and find three living things — a bird, a tree, a person. Linger on each. Fromm would call this an exercise in biophilia.

fomo.text: “Do I actually need this?” Marcuse saw this simple question as the beginning of freedom. The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives while you are somewhere you shouldn’t be is very common, and it isn’t only about you. Fromm described the “marketing orientation” of character: a person begins to perceive themselves as a commodity to be presented advantageously and constantly checks how others are “selling.” In One-Dimensional Man (1964), Marcuse showed that a vast choice of goods, experiences and entertainment does not in itself mean freedom: it may simply keep us in the race. Then the fear of missing out is largely a manufactured feeling: the system wins when we always feel that real life is somewhere else. This removes part of the guilt. That is why Marcuse’s question is worth asking again and again.
fomo.practice: Put your phone face down for five minutes and simply be where you are: sounds, light, your own breathing. This is the life that can’t be missed.

quote.text: Free choice among a wide variety of goods and services does not signify freedom if these goods and services sustain social controls over a life of toil and fear.
quote.author: Herbert Marcuse

sleepless.text: Extending Marcuse’s thought, even the night today is subject to the “performance principle.” Hours without sleep, with thoughts going round in circles, are lonely enough — and on top of that comes the fear of missing your quota. Sleep has become a resource to be properly replenished so that you work well tomorrow — and the anxiety “I won’t get enough sleep” itself keeps you awake. In his essay “Free Time” (1969), Adorno observed that even our rest is organized on the model of work. Perhaps your nighttime thoughts are what found no room during the day. So you don’t have to demand efficiency from the night. It isn’t an exam. Even quiet rest without sleep is still rest.
sleepless.practice: Keep a sheet of paper by the bed and write each circling thought down in one line — let the night hand them over to the morning for safekeeping. Tell yourself: “I’ll look in the morning.”

betrayal.text: Adorno called “coldness” the basic principle of life in a competitive society: everyone learns to protect their own interest first. When you are betrayed, you may feel that cold for the first time where the warmth of trust used to be. Fromm described how relationships in such a society begin to resemble exchange — “you scratch my back, I’ll scratch yours.” If so, betrayal is the moment when the logic of advantage or fear suddenly invades a relationship you thought was alive. This explains, but doesn’t excuse. And one more thing: the fact that you trusted is not naivety but that very capacity for living connection which the Frankfurt thinkers considered the most precious thing in a human being. You don’t have to give it up along with the loss.
betrayal.practice: Read aloud Adorno’s line: “Tenderness between people is nothing other than awareness of the possibility of relations without purpose.” Think of one person with whom you have exactly such a relationship.

jealousy.text: Fromm described mature love as a paradox: two beings become one and yet remain two. Jealousy often grows where that “two” is frightening: you are afraid of losing what is dearest. In To Have or to Be? (1976), Erich Fromm distinguished two ways of living: “having” and “being.” In the having mode, a loved one quietly becomes something you have and that can be taken away — and then any shadow of a threat triggers panic. In this light, jealousy is not proof of bad character but the voice of the anxiety of having, which everyone has. There’s no need to be ashamed of it. But you can notice where love says “you’re mine” and try to translate it into the language of being: “being with you is precious to me.”
jealousy.practice: Silently translate one jealous sentence from the language of having into the language of being: instead of “you’re mine” — “I treasure being with you.” Say the new version to yourself and notice what changes in your body.

resentment.text: In Escape from Freedom (1941) Fromm noticed a pattern: bitterness, hostility and the wish to pay back grow where life is cramped and cannot unfold. If you have carried a resentment for a long time, you really were hurt once. The less room there is in a life for what is alive, the stronger the pull toward destruction. This is not a reproach to you, nor a demand that you forgive right away. It is a thought about where to look for relief: less in arguing with the person who hurt you inside your head, and more in widening your own life. Resentment keeps your gaze chained to the past. Fromm would suggest asking what else in your life is waiting for your attention and energy.
resentment.practice: Go for a short walk and give it entirely to what belongs only to your life: the street, the sky, your own steps. The argument with the one who hurt you can wait.

quote.text: Destructiveness is the outcome of unlived life.
quote.author: Erich Fromm

heartbreak.text: Fromm thought the great mistake of our time is to treat love as a problem of the “object”: find the right person and the job is done. When a relationship ends, it feels as if a piece has been torn out of your life — and love itself along with it. But for Fromm love is first of all a capacity, an activity, an “art” that lives within the person. He distinguished “falling in love” — the sudden collapse of the walls between people — from the ability to love, which stays with us even when a relationship has ended. So you have lost a particular person and a shared life with them, and that is a real loss that needs to be mourned. But you haven’t lost the capacity to love: it is yours, and your pain is one of its signs.
heartbreak.practice: Put your palm on your chest and feel your heart beating under it. Say to yourself: “The capacity to love is in me, not in the other person.” Stay like this for a minute.

impostor.text: “I am as you desire me” — Fromm liked to quote this Pirandello title because he saw in it the formula of a whole age. The fear of being found out any minute often visits those who are doing perfectly well. In Man for Himself (1947), Erich Fromm described the “marketing orientation”: in a society where everything is for sale, a person begins to feel like a commodity, and to experience their worth as a “price” set by others. Then one’s sense of self becomes shaky: today I was valued, tomorrow I may be revalued. This means impostor syndrome is not your secret worthlessness but a natural consequence of a life in which worth is measured by demand. Fromm saw a footing in the “productive orientation” — in what you actually do and feel, not in someone else’s assessment.
impostor.practice: Do one small piece of your work right now for its own sake — not for a report and not for anyone’s eyes — and notice what that feels like. Fromm called this the productive orientation.

self_hatred.text: “Loving yourself is selfishness”: Fromm considered this familiar idea one of the most harmful and argued against it in Man for Himself (1947). If your inner voice is merciless right now, you deserve gentleness — including your own. Fromm showed the opposite: respect and love for oneself and for others don’t compete but go together, and a person who can’t be kind to themselves has a hard time being kind to others. The inner critic, in Fromm’s view, often speaks with the voice of the “authoritarian conscience” — internalized demands of others — rather than your own “humanistic conscience,” which cares about your growth. Adorno added that real love is a place where you can be weak. Such a place can begin to be built inside yourself as well.
self_hatred.practice: Imagine your best friend saying this inner critic’s sentence about themselves. What would you answer them? Say it aloud — to yourself.

quote.text: You are loved only where you may show yourself weak without provoking strength.
quote.author: Theodor Adorno

helplessness.text: Adorno called our time an “administered world”: much is decided somewhere far away — in markets, corporations, states. If you feel you can’t change anything, that is heavy, and it deserves to be taken seriously. Fromm, in Escape from Freedom (1941), had already shown how small and powerless a person feels in such a world. In other words, your helplessness is partly a sober perception of reality, not your personal inadequacy. But in his essay “Resignation” (1969), Adorno insisted that even when action is almost impossible, the very capacity to think clearly and to disagree is not capitulation. You may not be able to change everything and still keep your own view, and the small acts that remain in your hands.
helplessness.practice: Right now, do one small thing that is surely in your hands: wash a cup, open a window, answer one message. For Adorno, not giving in is already an act.

procrastination.text: “The performance principle” was Marcuse’s name for an invisible overseer that demands life be useful above all. When you just can’t get started, it’s easy to accuse yourself of laziness, but the Frankfurt thinkers would suggest a wider view. In Eros and Civilization (1955) he showed: our lives are more and more subordinated to the demand to be useful and efficient, and work is often experienced as something alien, imposed. Fromm spoke of alienation — a state in which a person doesn’t recognize themselves in what they do. If so, procrastination is sometimes a quiet resistance: part of you doesn’t want to give its energy to something in which it doesn’t feel itself. This isn’t a reason to drop everything but a reason to listen. Sometimes it’s enough to find even a tiny piece of the task that you do for yourself rather than for an evaluation.
procrastination.practice: Find the smallest piece of the task that interests you yourself and spend five minutes on it — as play, not as a quota. Marcuse dreamed of work that resembles play.

uprooted.text: “Reflections from Damaged Life” is the subtitle Adorno gave Minima Moralia, a book written in exile. Almost all the Frankfurt thinkers — Adorno, Horkheimer, Marcuse, Fromm — were forced to leave Germany in the 1930s. When the ground has gone from under your feet, it is a deep loss, even if the decision was right. Adorno knew this first-hand. Adorno acknowledged the pain of homelessness but also saw a special kind of knowledge in it: whoever has lost their home sees more clearly that the familiar order of things is not the only possible one. Then your uprootedness is not only a wound but also a new lens. It doesn’t cancel the longing, but it lets you not feel a stranger to everything in the world.
uprooted.practice: Walk around the place where you now live and find one thing the locals don’t notice but you do, because you came from outside. Adorno considered the exile’s gaze a special kind of knowledge.

quote.text: It is part of morality not to be at home in one’s home.
quote.author: Theodor Adorno

overload.text: Adorno and Horkheimer described a factory that turns out not machines but entertainment and news — the “culture industry,” where everything is standardized, fast and replaceable. The endless feed is tiring, and this is not your inability to “keep up.” They observed that this industry constantly promises satisfaction and constantly postpones it, which is why you keep wanting more. Marcuse added that a stream of ready-made impressions leaves less and less room for one’s own thought. If so, overload is not a personal weakness but a natural reaction to an environment designed to hold your attention. Stepping away from part of the stream is not fleeing the world but reclaiming your right to think at your own pace.
overload.practice: Close the feed and sit for two minutes with nothing new coming in. Catch one thought that arrived on its own, not from a screen — Marcuse would call it truly yours.

unreality.text: Adorno spoke of “reification”: in a world where much is turned into commodity and function, living relationships begin to seem like things, and people like roles. If everything around you, or you yourself, feels somehow not quite real, it is strange and frightening, and it deserves gentle care. Marcuse wrote of a “one-dimensional” world where everything is predictable and packaged in advance. In such a world, a sense of unreality may also be a signal of too little living contact, not only a glitch in perception. This doesn’t explain everything, but it lets you not be frightened of yourself: perhaps you are keenly feeling what many people have stopped noticing.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a pronounced texture — fabric, wood, cold water — and name three sensations aloud. A small return from things-as-functions to the living world.

awe.text: In Aesthetic Theory (1970), Adorno chose the word “shudder” for the instant when art or nature knocks a person out of being closed in on themselves, and they feel something greater. The awe you are feeling belongs to these rare instants. Adorno even wrote that the aesthetic relationship is ultimately defined by the capacity for such a shudder. For Adorno this experience is valuable because it cannot be fully bought, packaged or put to use. In this light, awe is one form of freedom: in these minutes you meet the world not as a consumer or a worker but as a living person. You can simply let it be.
awe.practice: Stay with what stirred your awe for one more minute, without photographing it or telling anyone. For Adorno, what matters is precisely what can’t be bought or packaged.

relief.text: In Eros and Civilization (1955), Marcuse distinguished two kinds of repression: the necessary kind, without which shared life is impossible, and “surplus” repression — an excess load demanded not by nature or other people but by the way society is organized. When something heavy finally lets go, it deserves to be noticed, without rushing on. So relief is a moment when part of this excess load falls away, and for an instant you feel how much strength went into holding on. The experience also tells you what life could be like with a lighter load. You can simply enjoy it — and remember while you’re at it: this lightness is not an accidental luxury but something you truly need.
relief.practice: Breathe out deeply and notice where your body has grown lighter. Rest your attention there for a few breaths — let the body remember what life without the excess load is like.

calm.text: “Lying on the water and looking peacefully at the sky” — this is how Adorno in Minima Moralia (1951) pictured a different happiness, free of endless growth and achievement. He argued against the ideal of unceasing activity, in which even rest must be useful. Calm is rare in the modern world, and it can be cherished. Marcuse spoke of the “pacification of existence” as the goal of a free society: a life in which one doesn’t have to fight all the time. This means your calm is neither idleness nor wasted time but a touch of what, in the end, makes doing anything worthwhile at all. It doesn’t need to be justified by usefulness.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute looking out the window or at the sky, and do nothing — don’t even check whether you are resting “correctly.”

quote.text: Rien faire comme une bête, lying on water and looking peacefully at the sky…
quote.author: Theodor Adorno

inspiration.text: Marcuse devoted his last book, The Aesthetic Dimension (1977), to one idea: art and imagination can show a world that doesn’t coincide with what is. The moment when you want to create and thought flows on its own is of the same nature. In To Have or to Be? (1976), Erich Fromm linked such moments to the mode of “being”: a person isn’t accumulating or appropriating but vividly, actively expressing themselves. He called this “productive” activity and distinguished it from mere busyness: you can be very busy and still create nothing of your own. In other words, inspiration is not a whim but an expression of your capacity for freedom. It doesn’t have to be turned into a result right away — it is enough to give it room.
inspiration.practice: Write down what has just come, as it is — no editing, no judging, a draft for yourself. Fromm would say: this is being, not having.

schadenfreude.text: Donald Duck gets his thrashing so that viewers grow used to the blows that come their own way — this is how Adorno and Horkheimer explained laughter at someone else’s misfortune in Dialectic of Enlightenment (1947). If you have caught yourself gloating, it is embarrassing to admit even to yourself. Where life is built on competition, someone else’s fall is felt for a moment as relief: so it isn’t me. Fromm would probably add that this is how the tension a competitive society builds up in everyone breaks through. Schadenfreude, then, is not your corruption but a trace of a system in which people are constantly compared. You can notice it and ask: what pressure of my own did it give me a break from?
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: in which area of life am I being compared most right now? Imagine for a minute that there is no ranking there at all. What would you do then?

contempt.text: In 1950 Adorno and his colleagues published The Authoritarian Personality and showed something unexpected: contempt for “the weak” often grows out of fear of one’s own weakness. Contempt seems confident and cold, but tension hides behind it. Fromm described the “marketing orientation”: when a person’s worth is measured by success and demand, it’s easy to start dividing people into “winners” and “losers” — and to look down on the latter. We reject in others, they observed, what we fear in ourselves. Then contempt is not a trait of your character but a yardstick society slips to everyone. Instead of being ashamed of it, you can ask: by what scale am I judging this person right now — and would I myself measure up to that scale on a hard day?
contempt.practice: Picture this person on a hard day — tired, frightened, as a child. Hold the image for a minute. Adorno would suggest asking: isn’t it my own weakness I reject in them?

disgust.text: In Minima Moralia Adorno didn’t hide his disgust at falseness, huckstering and coldness — and treated it as a form of knowledge: sometimes it is the first to notice that something is wrong with the world. If you want to turn away from people, a situation or yourself right now, this strong bodily feeling doesn’t make you a bad person. In The Heart of Man (1964), Fromm distinguished “biophilia” — love of everything living and growing — from an attraction to what is dead, mechanical, frozen. If so, disgust can be a healthy reaction of a living person to what deadens. And then it matters to distinguish it from disgust at yourself, which is most often imposed from outside — by other people’s yardsticks and models. Disgust is worth listening to: what is it really pointing at?
disgust.practice: Breathe out slowly, turning slightly away as your body wants to, then turn back and silently name one word: what exactly is it rejecting — falseness, coldness, deadness?

revenge.text: Fromm described “revengeful violence” almost as magic: it seeks not to protect but to undo what happened. The wish for revenge usually grows out of a real hurt, and it has its own dignity: you don’t accept that you can be treated this way. Fromm observed that vengefulness is stronger the fewer other supports a person has — a productive life, love, a sense of their own strength. Hence his thought: the antidote to revenge is not suppression but the widening of life. In this light, you can fully acknowledge the wish for revenge without acting on it, and ask: what part of my life has this wound now blocked from view — and how can I get it back?
revenge.practice: Give a few minutes today to something that makes you stronger and more alive — movement, music, a talk with a friend. Fromm considered the widening of life the best antidote to revenge.

anger_at_loved.text: “The psychic agency of society” is what Fromm called the family: through it the pressure, fatigue and anxieties of the wider world reach us, and at home all this often spills out onto those nearest to us. In “Authority and the Family” (1936), Horkheimer showed how the family mirrors the power relations of the wider society. If anger at someone close burns and shame follows, that is very human. So your anger may be not only about this person but also about the load you are both carrying. Fromm considered love not a feeling that either “is there or isn’t” but an activity of care, responsibility and respect. Anger doesn’t cancel it; but it matters not to let it spill out, and instead to translate it into words and requests.
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger subsides, say one request to your loved one instead of a reproach: “I need…” Fromm considered love an activity, and a request is a small form of it.

quote.text: Love is the active concern for the life and the growth of that which we love.
quote.author: Erich Fromm

ambivalence.text: Adorno distrusted thinking that hurries to stick a single label on what is alive — “good” or “bad,” “I love” or “I don’t” — and called it “identity thinking.” Loving and being unable to stand the same person is exhausting, but it is a very human state. Adorno believed truth often lives precisely in a contradiction that shouldn’t be hastily resolved. In The Art of Loving, Fromm wrote that mature love is a union in which each person keeps their separateness; and where two separate people meet, friction is inevitable. This means mixed feelings are not a sign that the relationship is false but a sign that you see the other person whole, not just the convenient part of them.
ambivalence.practice: Say three sentences to yourself about this person, each containing both “I love” and “I can’t stand.” Adorno would call this refusing a false unity.

guilty_relief.text: In Man for Himself (1947), Fromm distinguished the “authoritarian conscience,” which punishes any “improper” feeling, from the “humanistic conscience,” which cares that you stay alive and whole. Relief after a breakup, the death of a loved one, or long, draining care for someone who is ill often brings shame — and here it matters which voice is speaking. After all, relief and love can live side by side. In other words, shame about relief speaks in the authoritarian voice: “you must feel nothing but grief.” The humanistic conscience may say something else: you carried a heavy load for a long time, and breathing out is the natural right of a living person. This doesn’t cancel your love or diminish the loss.
guilty_relief.practice: Take one long out-breath — the one you haven’t allowed yourself for so long. Say to yourself: “I carried a heavy load for a long time, and breathing out is my right.” It doesn’t cancel the love.

indifference.text: In 1966 Adorno gave a radio lecture, “Education after Auschwitz,” and named coldness as the chief affliction of modern people. If where you “ought” to be moved there is only silence inside, it’s frightening, but it doesn’t mean you are heartless. Adorno considered this coldness a problem not of individual character but of the whole social order. Then your indifference may be not emptiness but armor grown from overload. Adorno saw the first step not in shaming people but in coldness becoming aware of itself and its causes: understanding already makes it less all-powerful. Feelings can return once there is even a little safe space.
indifference.practice: Recall the last time you felt something strongly, even over something small, and go back there in your mind for a minute: what surrounded you, who was near?

escape.text: Fromm called it “alienation” when a person experiences their own life as someone else’s — as a set of roles. The urge to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — and start over often speaks in the voice of the living part of you, the part that has run out of room. In Eros and Civilization (1955), Marcuse wrote about the “performance principle”: society demands above all that we function — work, conform, never stop. If so, the urge to escape is not irresponsibility but the protest of what is alive against being turned into a function. It doesn’t call for immediate decisions at all. But it is worth listening to: it points to which parts of your life feel alien and which still feel like yours.
escape.practice: Walk through your usual week in your mind and notice where you live and where you merely function. Find at least one “I live” — it will show you what is worth keeping.

forbidden_attraction.text: Marcuse wrote of Eros as a life drive toward connection and fullness that doesn’t fit the frames society assigns it. Attraction to someone who is “off limits” can be confusing and frightening — but in itself it doesn’t make you bad, and it decides nothing for you. Extending his thought, where life is tightly compressed by obligations, this striving can suddenly flare up in an unexpected direction. In The Art of Loving, Fromm distinguished “falling in love,” which seizes us, from love as an activity — care, responsibility, respect and knowledge of the other. Attraction to the unavailable can be looked at as a message: what aliveness, what recognition or freedom is your life missing right now? The answer to that question remains yours.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Go for a five-minute walk and ask yourself on the way: what aliveness, recognition or freedom am I missing right now? The answer commits you to no decision.

social_anxiety.text: Fromm described a person who enters a room like goods laid out on a counter: will I be taken or not? This is what the “marketing orientation” looks like in a society where everything is for sale — and every appearance in public turns into a small exam. No wonder starting a conversation, speaking up or simply walking in can be so hard; this experience is very common. In this light, shyness is not only your personal trait but also a reaction to yardsticks society imposes on everyone. Fromm contrasted “having” and “being”: you don’t have to “have” a good impression; you can “be” in the conversation — take an interest in the other person, not only in how you look. This shift of attention brings noticeable relief.
social_anxiety.practice: In your next conversation, ask the other person one question whose answer genuinely interests you, and simply listen. Fromm would call this moving from “having an impression” to “being in the conversation.”

uncertainty.text: Calculate everything and leave nothing unknown — Adorno and Horkheimer saw this wish as the engine of all modern civilization. When the future is unclear and there is nothing to lean on, wanting to know in advance is natural. But they also noticed that the pursuit of total control doesn’t free us from fear; it gives rise to new forms of it. In Escape from Freedom, Fromm wrote that insecurity is an inevitable side of freedom, and many people flee from it toward authorities and ready-made answers. So the impossibility of knowing the future is not your personal failure but a shared condition of life from which no system is exempt. Bearing the unknown is also a form of freedom.
uncertainty.practice: Write two lines: what you can’t know in advance — and what you can do today, whatever the outcome.

quote.text: Man imagines himself free from fear when there is no longer anything unknown.
quote.author: Max Horkheimer, Theodor Adorno

waiting.text: In his essay “Free Time,” Adorno observed that the logic of work seeps even into leisure: time without useful activity feels lost. That is why waiting — for an answer, results, news — is doubly agonizing: everything is on pause, and it feels shameful to “waste” the pause. It is hard, and pretending not to care doesn’t work. In Eros and Civilization, Marcuse dreamed of time not subordinated to productivity alone — time for play, contemplation, unhurriedness. And while there is no answer yet, your time still belongs to you. It doesn’t need to be “killed” or hurried; it can be lived — without pretending you don’t care, but also without handing your whole life over to waiting.
waiting.practice: Give the next five minutes to play without purpose: doodle, dance to one song, rock on your chair. Marcuse dreamed of exactly this kind of time.

regret.text: Walter Benjamin, a friend of the Frankfurt School, described the angel of history in 1940: its face turned toward the past, it would like to stay, awaken the dead and make whole what has been smashed, but a storm drives it forward. If regret keeps coming back to you, you may recognize yourself in this angel. Benjamin believed the past is not definitively closed: remembrance can give it back its voice, and what was missed can still resonate in the present. This means regret is not useless self-torment but a memory of possibilities that haven’t entirely vanished. Some of them may come alive in a new form — in what you do now.
regret.practice: Find or recall Paul Klee’s drawing Angelus Novus, which Benjamin kept with him, and look at it for a minute. Ask: which missed possibility could still resonate today?

longing.text: In The Art of Loving (1956), Fromm held that the deepest human need is to overcome one’s “separateness,” and love is the chief answer to it. That is why, when someone you love isn’t near, you miss them almost physically: their voice, their presence, the familiar little things. This is the natural price of real connection. Fromm would call it a longing for a living relationship. In other words, longing is not weakness but evidence that you managed to truly connect with another. Fromm considered love a capacity of the person themselves, not only a bond with one object — so it doesn’t vanish with their absence and can show itself in care, attention, creativity. You can live through longing without driving it away.
longing.practice: Tell someone one story about this person — a funny or a warm one. Fromm saw love as a capacity, not only a bond with one person: in the telling, it goes on acting.

world_pain.text: In his later years Horkheimer spoke of “the longing for the wholly Other” — the hope that injustice will not have the last word. If pain for the world — for wars, injustice, grim news — weighs on you so much that it’s hard to live an ordinary life, it speaks of your capacity for compassion. Adorno, who lived through an age of catastrophes, insisted that suffering must be heard and expressed, not disguised. Then your pain is neither naivety nor weakness but a sign that you refuse to accept suffering as normal. But it is impossible to carry it alone. Pain shared with others and turned into even a small action becomes more bearable.
world_pain.practice: Talk about what troubles you in the world with someone you trust. Then choose one small good deed close at hand.

quote.text: Perennial suffering has as much right to expression as a tortured man has to scream.
quote.author: Theodor Adorno

rejection.text: Fromm observed that most people think of love as the problem of “being loved” — becoming attractive, earning being chosen — rather than as their own capacity to love. That is why rejection hurts as though it wasn’t a request that was turned down but you as a whole. In a society arranged like a market, a refusal is easily experienced as “I wasn’t bought,” as if a price had been put on you. If so, it is worth reminding yourself: you are not goods in a shop window, and someone’s refusal doesn’t determine your worth. It says that this particular meeting didn’t work out, not what you are worth. Your capacity to love, to be a friend, to take an interest in the world stays with you, whatever the other person answered.
rejection.practice: Complete the sentence in writing: “I wasn’t chosen for…, but I can still…” — and list three things. For Fromm, this is your capacity to love, bought by no one.

abandonment.text: “Symbiotic union” is what Fromm called the attempt to dissolve into another so as never to be alone again. In Escape from Freedom he showed how modern people, freed from the old solid ties, were left alone with the anxiety of aloneness. The fear of being abandoned can run very deep: it seems that without the other there will be nothing to hold on to. Fromm believed that such a bond, based on fear, makes us even more vulnerable. He described mature love as the union of two people, each of whom preserves their own integrity. In this light, working with the fear lies not in clinging more tightly to the other but in gradually strengthening your connection with yourself too: your interests, your supports, your life.
abandonment.practice: Today, do one thing that belongs only to you: take your favorite route, get on with your own pursuit, call a different friend. Fromm would say: this is how your own wholeness grows stronger.

unrequited.text: “Love is primarily giving, not receiving,” Fromm wrote in The Art of Loving. When the feeling is there but no answer comes, it wounds painfully, but that doesn’t make the love any less real. Fromm stressed this again and again. Fromm considered the capacity to love a strength of the one who loves, not a reward for reciprocity. So your love is neither a mistake nor a defeat: it shows that you are capable of deep feeling. It hurts that right now it has found no answer, and that pain is worth living through without rushing yourself. But the capacity that showed itself in this love stays with you — and one day it may find another, mutual path.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love has awakened in you: which qualities, which wishes. For Fromm, this is your own power, and it isn’t going anywhere.

quote.text: Love is an activity, not a passive affect; it is a “standing in,” not a “falling for.”
quote.author: Erich Fromm

humiliation.text: Axel Honneth, an heir of the Frankfurt School, described in The Struggle for Recognition (1992) three things without which it is hard for a person to respect themselves: love from those close to them, respect for their rights, and esteem for their contribution. Humiliation takes one of them away — often in front of others — which is why it wounds so deeply. This pain is natural and says nothing about your weakness. Humiliation is a form of “misrecognition”: denying a person what is due to them as a person. But Honneth also saw in the experience of misrecognition a source of resistance: the pain of humiliation shows that you know what you deserve. This means your pain is the voice of your dignity.
humiliation.practice: Get in touch with someone who respects you — for no reason, just to talk. Honneth would say: the wounds of misrecognition are healed by recognition.

body_shame.text: “Interest in the Body” is the title Adorno and Horkheimer gave a note in Dialectic of Enlightenment, where they showed that civilization both exalts and despises the body, turning it into an object to be managed. If the mirror has become an exam, that is exhausting, and it isn’t only about you. Adorno would call this someone else’s yardstick passed off as your own. The culture industry, Adorno would add, constantly supplies model bodies and faces by which we begin to measure ourselves. In other words, your shame is not only your problem but the imprint of yardsticks imposed on everyone. You can give your body back its place: not a commodity or a project, but a living self that feels, moves, rejoices.
body_shame.practice: For a minute, be in your body from the inside: warmth, breath, weight. Notice one pleasant sensation that doesn’t depend on appearance — the body is not an object but a living self.

illness.text: Adorno wrote of the “somatic moment” of thought: physical suffering tells cognition that suffering ought not to be. If your body lets you down — illness, pain, weakness — irritation, fear and sadness are natural here. For him, bodily pain is not a trifle beside the “higher” questions but the place where honest philosophy begins. Fromm would probably add that a society living in the “having” mode teaches us to treat the body as property that is obliged to work properly — and then illness is experienced as a breakdown and a disgrace. But illness is not your fault and not a failure. Your pain has a right to be heard, and you have a right to care, not to reproaches from yourself.
illness.practice: Say aloud to yourself one sentence you would say to a sick friend — gentle, with no demands. Adorno believed suffering needs to be heard, not shamed.

pride.text: In Man for Himself (1947), Fromm described the “productive orientation” — a person’s capacity to put their powers to use: to create, to understand, to care. He distinguished “marketing” pride from “productive” pride: the first depends on how you are assessed, the second on the very activity in which you expressed yourself. What you are feeling now is well earned, and there’s no need to hide it. Fromm considered healthy self-love not selfishness but a condition for loving others. Then your pride is joy at having become a little more yourself. You can enjoy it without waiting for anyone else’s assessment, and notice which of your powers came alive in this work.
pride.practice: Tell someone not about the result but about the process: what was hard and what came alive in you along the way. Fromm would consider the second part more important than the first.

quote.text: Man’s main task in life is to give birth to himself, to become what he potentially is.
quote.author: Erich Fromm

melancholy.text: “The melancholy science” is what Adorno called his Minima Moralia, echoing Nietzsche’s Gay Science: a thoughtful look at life is inevitably tinged with sorrow for what it could have been. Bright sadness, in which sorrow is mixed with tenderness toward the world, doesn’t need fixing. Adorno knew this feeling intimately. In his book on German baroque drama (1928), Benjamin saw melancholy as a special form of attention: the melancholic lingers over things and notices in them what a hurried glance misses. If so, bright sadness is not a malfunction but a way of seeing more deeply. You can live it like slow music, without letting it turn into despair.
melancholy.practice: Choose one object nearby and look at it slowly for a minute, like Benjamin’s melancholic. Notice what you hadn’t noticed before.
